client: I've been feeling really overwhelmed at work lately. I was just assigned this challenging project with a tight deadline, and on top of that, our team is short-staffed, which makes everything feel even more stressful. I’m starting to wonder if therapy can really help me manage all this pressure.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a heavy load at work right now, and it's completely understandable to feel overwhelmed with so much on your plate. Juggling a challenging project and a short-staffed team can feel really stressful. Let's explore some of the thoughts you're having about this pressure—what specific beliefs are coming up for you about your ability to handle the situation?

client: I guess one of the main thoughts I have is that I’m not good enough to manage this project. I keep worrying that I'm going to mess things up and let my team down, especially since we’re already short-staffed. It’s frustrating because I want to believe I can handle it, but the pressure just makes me doubt myself even more.
therapist: I can see how frustrating it must be to feel that way, especially when you want to believe in your abilities but the pressure is making you doubt yourself. It’s common to experience self-doubt in challenging situations, particularly when you feel like the stakes are high. What evidence do you have that supports the idea that you might not be good enough, and how might you counter those thoughts with some alternative perspectives?

client: I guess the evidence comes from a few past experiences where I struggled with deadlines or didn't meet expectations, which makes me think I might fail again. But I also realize that I've had successes too, like when I led a previous project and it turned out well. It’s just hard to focus on those positive experiences when the anxiety kicks in, and I’m not sure how to really reframe my thinking when I'm in the middle of all this stress.
therapist: It sounds like you're caught in a tough cycle of focusing on past struggles while trying to remember the successes you've had. That anxiety can really cloud your judgment and make it hard to see your strengths. What if we worked on some strategies to help you shift your focus to those positive experiences, especially when the stress starts to build? How would it feel to remind yourself of those successes in the moment?

client: I can see how that might help, but it just feels really difficult to actually do in the moment. When the stress hits, all I can think about is the pressure and the fear of failing, and I struggle to remember those successes. I’m not sure I would be able to shift my focus like that when I'm feeling so overwhelmed.
therapist: It sounds like the overwhelming feelings make it really tough to access those positive memories when you need them the most. It's completely normal to feel that way under pressure, and it's okay to acknowledge how difficult it can be. Maybe we can explore some simple techniques you can use to ground yourself in those moments of stress, like a quick breathing exercise or a mantra that reminds you of your strengths. What do you think might work for you when those feelings start to arise?

client: I think a breathing exercise could be helpful, but I’m not sure if I’ll remember to do it when I’m stressed. It feels like my mind just goes blank under pressure, and I get so caught up in the moment that I forget about any techniques I might have learned. A mantra sounds nice, but I’m worried it won’t really resonate with me when I’m feeling overwhelmed.
therapist: It sounds really challenging to think about using techniques when your mind feels blank under pressure. That can make it tough to trust that these tools will actually help you in those moments. Perhaps we can work together to find a simple mantra or breathing technique that feels personal and meaningful to you, so it might be easier to recall when you're feeling overwhelmed. What kind of phrases or ideas resonate with you that could serve as a reminder of your strengths?

client: I'm not really sure what phrases would resonate with me. I guess I’d like something that reminds me that I can handle challenges, but it feels hard to come up with anything in this moment. I worry that if I pick something and it doesn't work, it’ll just add to my frustration instead of helping me when I need it most.
therapist: It sounds like you're feeling a bit stuck trying to find the right phrase, and that uncertainty can be frustrating. It's completely understandable to worry about choosing something that might not resonate when you're feeling overwhelmed. How about we start with a very simple phrase, like "I can handle this," and see if that feels manageable for you? We can always adjust it later if it doesn’t resonate when you’re in the moment. What do you think about starting there?

client: Starting with "I can handle this" feels a bit better, but I still have doubts. What if I say it and don’t believe it in the moment? I want to feel confident, but I’m worried that repeating a phrase won’t actually change how I feel under pressure. It just seems like it might not be enough to really help me when things get tough.
therapist: It’s great to hear that starting with "I can handle this" feels a bit better, but I understand your concerns about whether it will truly help you in the moment. Doubts can make it hard to fully believe in a mantra, especially when you're feeling pressure. Let's explore how you can build that confidence over time, perhaps by combining the mantra with some small successes you’ve had in the past. What are some small wins you’ve experienced recently that could reinforce that belief in yourself?

client: I think I’ve had a few small wins, like when I solved a tricky problem for a client last week or when I received positive feedback from my manager on my last report. But even those feel so small compared to the challenges I’m facing now. I guess it’s hard to connect those little successes to the bigger pressure I’m feeling, and I worry that they won’t be enough to help me believe in the mantra when I really need it.
therapist: It's understandable to feel like those small wins might not measure up to the bigger challenges you're facing right now. It can be tough to connect those moments of success to the pressure you’re feeling, especially when everything feels overwhelming. Perhaps we can explore ways to celebrate those small victories more fully, so they become part of your inner strength when you're under pressure. How might you acknowledge those achievements in a way that feels meaningful to you?

client: I’m not really sure how to celebrate those small victories in a way that feels meaningful. It feels like I should just move on to the next task instead of taking time to acknowledge what I’ve done. I worry that if I start focusing on those small successes, I’ll lose sight of the bigger challenges that are still ahead of me, and that feels risky.
therapist: I can see why it feels challenging to take the time to celebrate your small victories when you're focused on the next task ahead. It's natural to worry that acknowledging those moments might distract you from the bigger challenges. What if we considered finding a balance—perhaps a brief moment to recognize those wins without losing sight of your goals? How might you incorporate a quick acknowledgment, like a note to yourself or a small ritual, that allows you to appreciate your progress while still moving forward?

client: I like the idea of finding a balance, but I'm still not sure how to fit that into my busy routine. A note to myself sounds okay, but I worry that I might forget to do it or that it won’t really make a difference. It just feels like one more thing to add to my plate, and I’m already feeling so overwhelmed with everything going on at work.
therapist: It sounds like you're feeling a bit skeptical about adding anything new to your routine, especially when you're already feeling overwhelmed. That’s completely understandable; it can be hard to find room for anything extra when there’s so much going on. What if we considered something very simple, like taking just a minute at the end of your day to reflect on one positive thing that happened? It doesn’t have to be a big gesture—just a small pause might help you recognize your progress without adding pressure. How does that sound to you?
